```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.8,
  fig.align = "center"
)
library(distmer)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

Fixed effects describe systematic differences in community composition. In
mixed-model language they are the population-level relationships we want to
estimate or test: habitat, treatment, season, environmental gradients, and
their interactions.

Type I, II, and III are not competing algorithms. They specify different
questions when predictor subspaces overlap. In a perfectly orthogonal design
they coincide; with unequal cells, correlation, or interactions they need not.

## Mite communities along environmental gradients

The `vegan::mite` data contain 35 oribatid mite taxa from 70 samples. For a
compact factorial example we combine the recorded topographic class with
tertiles of water content. Categorising a continuous variable is only for this
illustration; an ecological analysis would usually keep water content numeric.

```{r mite-data}
data(mite, mite.env, package = "vegan")
mite_bray <- vegdist(mite, method = "bray")

breaks <- quantile(mite.env$WatrCont, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1))
env <- transform(
  mite.env,
  Wetness = cut(
    WatrCont, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE,
    labels = c("dry", "intermediate", "wet")
  ),
  Topo = droplevels(factor(Topo))
)
with(env, table(Wetness, Topo))
```

All six combinations occur, but their sample sizes differ. The ordination
suggests that both predictors may contribute to composition.

```{r mite-plot}
ord <- as.data.frame(cmdscale(mite_bray, k = 2))
names(ord) <- c("Axis1", "Axis2")
ord$Wetness <- env$Wetness
ord$Topo <- env$Topo

ggplot(ord, aes(Axis1, Axis2, colour = Wetness, shape = Topo)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Oribatid mite communities",
    subtitle = "Bray-Curtis principal coordinates",
    x = "PCoA axis 1", y = "PCoA axis 2"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Type I: a sequential question

Type I asks what each term adds at the point where it enters the formula. The
question is explicitly ordered:

```{r type-one}
wetness_first <- permanova(
  mite_bray ~ Wetness * Topo, env,
  type = "I", permutations = 499, seed = 11
)

topography_first <- permanova(
  mite_bray ~ Topo * Wetness, env,
  type = "I", permutations = 499, seed = 11
)

wetness_first$table[1:3, c("Source", "df", "Pseudo-F", "P(perm)")]
topography_first$table[1:3, c("Source", "df", "Pseudo-F", "P(perm)")]
```

Use Type I when order expresses the scientific model: for example, adjust for
a pre-treatment gradient before asking what treatment adds. Do not choose an
order because it produces the smaller p-value.

## Type II: population effects respecting marginality

Type II tests a main effect after terms that do not contain it, while holding
its containing interactions out of that reduced model. In an additive model it
is the familiar question “what does this predictor add after the other
predictors?” and is invariant to formula order.

```{r type-two}
fit_II <- permanova(
  mite_bray ~ Wetness * Topo, env,
  type = "II", permutations = 499, seed = 11
)
fit_II$table[1:3, c("Source", "df", "Pseudo-F", "P(perm)")]
```

Type II is often a sensible default for ecological main effects when unequal
cell counts are incidental and the interaction is not the main target.

## Type III: each term conditional on every other term

Type III keeps all other terms, including interactions, in the reduced model.
A main effect is then a contrast at the reference implied by the factor coding.
With interactions this requires sum-to-zero contrasts; `permanova()` applies
them to a copy of the data so the original data frame is not modified.

```{r type-three}
fit_III <- permanova(
  mite_bray ~ Wetness * Topo, env,
  type = "III", permutations = 499, seed = 11
)
fit_III$table[1:3, c("Source", "df", "Pseudo-F", "P(perm)")]
```

The three definitions can be compared directly:

```{r type-comparison}
fits <- list(I = wetness_first, II = fit_II, III = fit_III)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(type) {
  tab <- fits[[type]]$table
  keep <- is.finite(tab$`Pseudo-F`)
  data.frame(
    Type = type, Term = tab$Source[keep],
    PseudoF = tab$`Pseudo-F`[keep], P = tab$`P(perm)`[keep]
  )
}))

ggplot(comparison, aes(Term, PseudoF, fill = Type)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.72) +
  labs(
    title = "The hypothesis definition can change the test",
    x = NULL, y = "Pseudo-F"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Keep continuous predictors continuous

Ordinary numeric covariates can be combined with factors. Here water content
and substrate density remain on their measured scales:

```{r continuous}
gradient_fit <- permanova(
  mite_bray ~ Topo + WatrCont + SubsDens,
  data = env,
  type = "II", permutations = 499, seed = 21
)
gradient_fit$table[1:3, c("Source", "df", "Pseudo-F", "P(perm)")]
```

Standardising a predictor changes its coefficient scale but not the subspace
tested by a one-degree-of-freedom term. Transformations that change ordering or
linearity can change the ecological hypothesis and should be justified.

## Choosing the type

- **Type I:** order represents a planned sequence of adjustment.
- **Type II:** main effects are interpreted marginally while respecting their
  containing interactions.
- **Type III:** each term is tested conditional on every other estimable term.

Always state the type in the methods. If the conclusions depend strongly on
the choice, show that sensitivity and return to the biological question rather
than treating the three p-values as interchangeable answers.
